cse-1992-a-1-i.approach: Read the entered-variable map cell by cell to get the canonical expression in $A,B,C$, then merge minterms that differ in one variable.

steps.title: Read each cell
steps.body:
Cell $(B,C)=(0,0)$ is 1 for any $A$: term $\overline{B}\,\overline{C}$. Cell $(1,0)$ holds $\overline{A}$: term $\overline{A}B\overline{C}$. Cell $(1,1)$ holds $A$: term $ABC$. Cell $(0,1)$ is 0.

$$f=\overline{B}\,\overline{C}+\overline{A}B\overline{C}+ABC$$
In minterms of $(A,B,C)$: $\overline{B}\,\overline{C}=m_0+m_4$, $\overline{A}B\overline{C}=m_2$, $ABC=m_7$, so $f=\sum m(0,2,4,7)$.

steps.title: Merge adjacent minterms
steps.body: $m_0+m_4=\overline{B}\,\overline{C}$ and $m_0+m_2=\overline{A}\,\overline{C}$ (pair $000,010$). $m_7=111$ has no neighbour among $\{011,101,110\}$ in $f$, so it stays $ABC$.

steps.title: Minimal SOP
steps.body:
$$f=\overline{B}\,\overline{C}+\overline{A}\,\overline{C}+ABC$$
(7 literals; the unmerged form $\overline{B}\,\overline{C}+\overline{A}B\overline{C}+ABC$ is equivalent but uses 8.)

pitfalls: Treating the $\overline{A}$ and $A$ cells as don't-cares or as 1s.
Missing that $m_2$ can pair with $m_0$ to drop a literal.
cse-1992-a-1-i.verification: Truth table of the answer gives 1 exactly at $ABC=000,010,100,111$, i.e. $\sum m(0,2,4,7)$, matching the map.

cse-1992-a-1-ii.approach: Count Hamming check bits for single-error correction on 4 data bits, then add the overall parity bit that raises the minimum distance to 4, since detecting $t$ errors needs $d_{min}\ge t+1$.

steps.title: Bits for 1-bit correction
steps.body: Need $2^p\ge m+p+1$ with $m=4$: $p=2$ gives $4\ge7$ (no), $p=3$ gives $8\ge8$ (yes). So Hamming(7,4) has 3 check bits and $d_{min}=3$.

steps.title: Raise distance for 3-bit detection
steps.body:
Detecting $t$ errors requires $d_{min}\ge t+1$, so 3-bit detection needs $d_{min}=4$. Adding one overall parity bit to Hamming(7,4) gives the extended (8,4) code with $d_{min}=4$.

Extra parity bits $=3+1=4$; minimum distance $=4$.

steps.title: Note on the wording
steps.body: A distance-4 code can correct 1 error **or** detect 3 errors (or correct 1 and detect 2 at once). Correcting 1 and detecting 3 simultaneously would need $d_{min}\ge 1+3+1=5$; the intended answer is the standard extended Hamming code.

pitfalls: Stopping at 3 check bits, which only gives $d_{min}=3$ (detects 2).
Using $d\ge 2t+1$ (the correction bound) for detection.
cse-1992-a-1-ii.verification: Extended Hamming (8,4): every nonzero codeword has weight 4 or 8, so $d_{min}=4\ge3+1$.

cse-1992-a-1-iii.approach: A minimum clock frequency exists only when the chip stores state dynamically; stored charge must be refreshed by clocking before it leaks away.

steps.title: Where state is kept
steps.body: Many microprocessors (e.g. NMOS designs like the 8085) use dynamic circuits: internal registers and latches hold bits as charge on tiny gate/node capacitances instead of in static flip-flops.

steps.title: Why a lower limit
steps.body: That charge leaks through junctions in a few milliseconds or less. The clock periodically re-drives (refreshes) these nodes; if the clock is slower than the specified minimum, charge decays between edges and stored bits are lost.

answer.value: they use dynamic (MOS) circuits that store information as charge on capacitances, which leaks away if the clock is too slow

pitfalls: Confusing this with the upper limit, which is set by propagation delays.
cse-1992-a-1-iii.verification: Fully static CMOS designs (e.g. 80C85, many microcontrollers) are specified down to DC clock, consistent with the reason.

cse-1992-a-1-iv.approach: Prefetching is a simple two-stage pipeline: the bus fetches upcoming instructions while the CPU executes the current one.

steps.title: Without prefetch
steps.body: Each instruction is fetched from (slow) memory and only then executed, so the CPU idles during every fetch.

steps.title: With a prefetch queue
steps.body: While the execution unit works on the current instruction, the bus unit fills the buffer with the next instructions (e.g. the 8086 6-byte queue). The next instruction is usually already on-chip, so fetch time is hidden behind execution time.

answer.value: fetching of the next instructions is overlapped with the execution of the current instruction (fetch–execute pipelining), so the CPU need not wait for memory

pitfalls: A taken branch flushes the buffer, so the gain is not perfect.
cse-1992-a-1-iv.verification: Matches the BIU/EU split of the 8086, the classic example of instruction prefetch.

cse-1992-a-1-v.approach: Handshaking makes every transfer acknowledged: the sender does not move on until the receiver confirms it took the data.

steps.title: Sequence
steps.body: Transmitter places data and raises *data valid* (strobe). Receiver latches it and raises *data accepted* (acknowledge). Transmitter removes data/strobe; receiver drops acknowledge. Only then is the next item sent.

steps.title: Why reliable
steps.body: Because each item gets an explicit acknowledgement, the sender never overwrites unread data and adapts to the speed of the receiver.

answer.value: the receiver sends back an acknowledgement, and the transmitter waits for it before sending the next item

pitfalls: Strobe-only (one-way) control gives no confirmation, which is the problem handshaking solves.
cse-1992-a-1-v.verification: Standard two-wire (request/acknowledge) handshake as in parallel I/O interfaces.

cse-1992-a-1-vi.approach: Expanding opcodes: unused opcode patterns at each level are extended with the next address field. Count leftover patterns level by level.
cse-1992-a-1-vi.given:
| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Word | 11 bits |
| Address field | 4 bits |
| Two-address instr. | 5 |
| One-address instr. (intended) | 32 |

steps.title: Two-address level
steps.body: Opcode $=11-2\times4=3$ bits $\Rightarrow 2^3=8$ patterns. Used 5, free $8-5=3$.

steps.title: One-address level
steps.body: Each free pattern extends by 4 bits: $3\times2^4=48$ patterns. Used 32, free $48-32=16$.

steps.title: Zero-address level
steps.body: Each free pattern extends by the last 4 bits: $16\times2^4=256$.

pitfalls: The paper prints "32 two-address" twice; 32 two-address instructions are impossible with 8 patterns, so it must be 32 one-address instructions.

cse-1992-a-1-vii.approach: Pass one must know the size of every statement to assign addresses; macro calls only reveal their size once expanded.

steps.title: What pass one does
steps.body: Pass one advances the location counter by the length of each statement and enters every label with its address in the symbol table.

steps.title: Why expand there
steps.body: A macro call stands for an unknown number of statements, possibly containing labels. Until it is expanded, pass one cannot advance the location counter correctly or define those labels, so all later addresses would be wrong. Hence expansion must happen in pass one.

answer.value: the expanded code generates statements (and labels) whose sizes and addresses must be known in pass one to build the symbol table and advance the location counter

pitfalls: Expanding in pass two would leave pass-one addresses and the symbol table inconsistent.
cse-1992-a-1-vii.verification: Same reason a one-pass macro processor must see a definition before its call.

cse-1992-a-1-viii.approach: The location counter (LC) is the assembler's running address: it tells where the current statement will be placed.

steps.title: Role
steps.body: LC is initialised (by ORG/START) and incremented by each instruction or data length. Its current value is the address of the statement being processed.

steps.title: Use
steps.body: When a label is encountered, it is entered in the symbol table with the current LC value; generated code and data are placed at LC addresses.

answer.value: to keep track of the address of the current instruction/data so that addresses can be assigned to labels (symbol table) and to the generated code

pitfalls: It is not the run-time program counter; it exists only during assembly.
cse-1992-a-1-viii.verification: Matches the pass-one algorithm of a standard two-pass assembler.

cse-1992-a-1-ix.approach: With edges already sorted, Kruskal is just $m$ union-find operations; with union by rank and path compression this is near-linear.

steps.title: Remaining work
steps.body: Sorting ($O(m\log m)$) is skipped. For each of the $m$ edges do two FINDs and at most one UNION ($n-1$ unions in total).

steps.title: Cost
steps.body: With union by rank and path compression, $O(m)$ operations on $n$ elements cost $O(m\,\alpha(m,n))$, where $\alpha$ is the inverse Ackermann function ($\le4$ in practice). So the time is $O(m\,\alpha(m,n))$, effectively $O(m)$.

pitfalls: Quoting $O(m\log m)$, which includes the sorting the question removes.
With union by rank only (no path compression) it is $O(m\log n)$.
cse-1992-a-1-ix.verification: Tarjan's bound for $m$ union-find operations is $\Theta(m\,\alpha(m,n))$.

cse-1992-a-1-x.approach: Use Euler's formula with the fact that, in a simple planar graph, every face is bounded by at least 3 edges.

steps.title: Face count bound
steps.body: Each face has at least 3 edges on its boundary and each edge borders at most 2 faces: $3f\le2e$.

steps.title: Combine with Euler
steps.body: $n-e+f=2\Rightarrow f=2-n+e$. Then $3(2-n+e)\le2e\Rightarrow e\le3n-6$ (for $n\ge3$). Triangulations attain it.

pitfalls: For bipartite (triangle-free) planar graphs the bound is $2n-4$.
cse-1992-a-1-x.verification: $K_4$: $n=4$, $e=6=3\cdot4-6$; $K_5$ has $10>9$ edges, so it is non-planar.

cse-1992-a-2-i.approach: All four are commutative; test associativity with a small counterexample.

steps.title: AND, OR, XOR
steps.body: All three are both commutative and associative ($(a\oplus b)\oplus c=a\oplus(b\oplus c)$ = parity of the three).

steps.title: NAND
steps.body: Commutative: $\overline{ab}=\overline{ba}$. Take $a=0,b=0,c=1$: $(a\uparrow b)\uparrow c=1\uparrow1=0$ but $a\uparrow(b\uparrow c)=0\uparrow1=1$. Not associative.

optionAnalysis.reason: AND is associative.
OR is associative.
XOR is associative (result is the parity of all inputs).
Commutative, but $(0\uparrow0)\uparrow1=0\ne1=0\uparrow(0\uparrow1)$.

pitfalls: NOR fails associativity the same way.

cse-1992-a-2-ii.approach: A component is universal if it can build NOT and AND, given the constants 0 and 1.

steps.title: Multiplexer
steps.body: A 2:1 MUX $y=\overline{s}a+sb$: with $a=1,b=0$ it gives $\overline{s}$; with $a=0$ it gives $sb$ (AND). NOT+AND is complete.

steps.title: Half adder
steps.body: Outputs $S=x\oplus y$, $C=xy$. $S$ with $y=1$ gives $\overline{x}$; $C$ is AND. Complete.

steps.title: XOR only, OR only
steps.body: XOR gates (even with constants) only produce affine functions $c\oplus x_1\oplus\dots$, so no AND. OR gates are monotone, so no NOT.

optionAnalysis.reason: XOR circuits are linear (affine); they cannot form $xy$.
A 2:1 MUX yields NOT and AND with constant inputs.
Sum output gives NOT (XOR with 1), carry gives AND.
OR is monotone; it cannot invert.

pitfalls: Both B and C assume constant 0/1 inputs are available, which is standard.
cse-1992-a-2-ii.verification: Post's criteria: XOR is linear, OR is monotone; MUX and HA escape all five classes.

cse-1992-a-2-iii.approach: A bit-slice chip (e.g. AMD 2901) is a 4-bit slice of a CPU's data path (ALU + register file + shifter); word length comes from cascading slices, control comes from a separate microprogram sequencer.

steps.title: Cascading
steps.body: Slices are connected side by side, carry/shift lines chained, to get 8, 16, 32 … bit processors: (a) true.

steps.title: Speed vs word length
steps.body: Carry ripples through more slices as width grows (lookahead units reduce but do not remove this), so speed depends on the configured width: (b) false.

steps.title: What a slice contains
steps.body: A slice has only the data path; control (sequencer such as the 2909/2910 and microprogram memory) is external: (d) true. Statement (c) is not accepted: a program counter can be kept in the slice's register file and the sequencer itself has a microprogram counter.

optionAnalysis.reason: Designed to be cascaded to any multiple of the slice width.
Carry propagation across slices makes wider words slower.
A PC can be held in the slice registers, and the companion sequencer has a (micro)program counter; not a valid characterisation.
A slice is the ALU/register/shifter data path only; control is external.

pitfalls: (c) and (d) look similar; (d) states the architecture, (c) overreaches.
cse-1992-a-2-iii.verification: Consistent with the AMD 2900 family organisation (2901 data path, 2909/2910 sequencer).

cse-1992-a-2-iv.approach: PCHL jumps to an address computed at run time, which is exactly what a jump table for a multi-way branch needs.

steps.title: What PCHL gives
steps.body: An indirect jump: PC $\leftarrow$ HL, where HL can be computed (e.g. table base + 2·index, then load the stored address).

steps.title: Match to constructs
steps.body: A **case** statement selects one of many targets by a value, implemented as a jump table indexed by that value followed by PCHL. If-then-else and while need only conditional jumps to fixed targets; a call must also push a return address, which PCHL does not do.

optionAnalysis.reason: Two fixed targets: a conditional jump (JZ/JNZ) suffices.
A loop uses a conditional jump back to a fixed label.
Multi-way branch through a jump table needs a computed jump: PCHL.
CALL must save the return address; PCHL does not push anything.

pitfalls: Indirect calls need an extra push of the return address, so PCHL alone is not a call.
cse-1992-a-2-iv.verification: Standard 8085 idiom: index into table, load address into HL, PCHL.

cse-1992-a-2-v.approach: In asynchronous serial framing the start bit tells the receiver when a character begins and the stop bit marks its end.

steps.title: Start bit
steps.body: The idle line is 1; the 1→0 start-bit edge lets the receiver align its sampling clock to the character (sample at bit centres).

steps.title: Stop bit
steps.body: Returns the line to 1, giving a guaranteed edge for the next start bit. Both serve **synchronization** of each character.

optionAnalysis.reason: Error detection is done by the parity bit, not start/stop bits.
They carry no redundancy for correction.
They frame each character so the receiver can synchronise.
The overhead slowing transfer is a side effect, not the purpose.

pitfalls: A missing stop bit raises a framing error, but that is a by-product, not error detection in the coding sense.
cse-1992-a-2-v.verification: UART framing: start + 5–8 data + optional parity + stop.

cse-1992-a-2-vi.approach: Pick the option that has a polynomial algorithm; the others are classic NP-complete problems.

steps.title: NP-hard ones
steps.body: Hamiltonian circuit, 0/1 knapsack (decision version) and graph colouring ($k\ge3$) are NP-complete, hence NP-hard.

steps.title: Polynomial one
steps.body: Biconnected components are found by one DFS computing discovery times and low values (Hopcroft–Tarjan) in $O(V+E)$. A problem in P is not NP-hard unless $P=NP$.

answer.value: (c) Finding bi-connected components of a graph

optionAnalysis.reason: Hamiltonian circuit is NP-complete.
0/1 knapsack is NP-complete (pseudo-polynomial DP only).
Solvable in $O(V+E)$ with DFS low-links.
Graph $k$-colouring is NP-complete for $k\ge3$.

pitfalls: The $O(nW)$ knapsack DP is not polynomial in the input size.

cse-1992-a-2-vii.approach: Build the tree bottom-up: group the 9 leaves into parents of 2 or 3 children, then group those parents, until one root remains. All leaves are at the same depth, so each level is grouped as a whole.

steps.title: Parents of the leaves
steps.body: $k$ parents need $2k\le9\le3k$, so $k=3$ (3+3+3) or $k=4$ (3+2+2+2).

steps.title: Case $k=3$
steps.body: 3 nodes need $k'$ parents with $2k'\le3\le3k'$: $k'=1$, the root. Internal nodes $=3+1=4$.

steps.title: Case $k=4$
steps.body: 4 nodes: $2k'\le4\le3k'$ gives $k'=2$; then 2 nodes have the root. Internal nodes $=4+2+1=7$.

steps.title: Result
steps.body: Possible counts are $\{4,7\}$, so (a) and (d).

optionAnalysis.reason: Root with 3 children, each with 3 leaves: $1+3=4$.
No level structure gives 5 internal nodes.
No level structure gives 6 internal nodes.
Leaves 3+2+2+2 under 4 nodes, under 2 nodes, under the root: $4+2+1=7$.

pitfalls: Forgetting the equal-depth rule: leaves and internal nodes cannot be mixed at one level.
cse-1992-a-2-vii.verification: Case 4: $3\cdot3=9$ leaves. Case 7: $3+2+2+2=9$ leaves with level sizes $1,2,4$.

cse-1992-a-2-viii.approach: By Kuratowski, the smallest non-planar graphs are $K_5$ and $K_{3,3}$; the one with fewest vertices is $K_5$.

steps.title: Up to 4 vertices
steps.body: Every graph on $\le4$ vertices is a subgraph of $K_4$, which is planar.

steps.title: 5 vertices
steps.body: Planar on 5 vertices allows $e\le3\cdot5-6=9$ edges, and $K_5$ minus an edge (9 edges) is planar. So the only non-planar 5-vertex graph is $K_5$: 5 vertices, $\binom52=10$ edges.

optionAnalysis.reason: $K_{3,3}$ is non-planar but has 6 vertices, not the minimum.
$K_4$ (6 edges, 4 vertices) is planar.
$K_5$: minimum vertex count for non-planarity.
$K_5-e$ (9 edges, 5 vertices) is planar.

pitfalls: Choosing $K_{3,3}$ because it has fewer edges; the question minimises vertices.

cse-1992-a-2-ix.approach: Comparison sorts need $\Omega(n\log n)$; radix sort with base $n$ handles keys up to $n^3$ in a constant number of linear passes.

steps.title: Comparison sorts
steps.body: Heapsort, quicksort and mergesort are comparison-based: $\Omega(n\log n)$ in the worst case.

steps.title: Radix sort in base $n$
steps.body: Write each key minus 1 (range $0..n^3-1$) in base $n$: exactly 3 digits. Each pass is a counting sort over $n$ digit values: $O(n+n)=O(n)$. Total $3\cdot O(n)=O(n)$.

optionAnalysis.reason: Comparison sort: $\Theta(n\log n)$.
Comparison sort: $O(n^2)$ worst, $O(n\log n)$ average.
Comparison sort: $\Theta(n\log n)$.
Base-$n$ radix sort: 3 passes of $O(n)$ counting sort.

pitfalls: Plain counting sort over $[1..n^3]$ costs $O(n^3)$; base-$n$ digits are the key.
Radix sort in base 2 or 10 would need $O(\log n)$ passes.
cse-1992-a-2-ix.verification: CLRS: $n$ keys of $b$ bits sort in $O((b/\log n)\,n)$; here $b=3\log n$ gives $O(n)$.

cse-1992-a-2-x.approach: Each P (wait) decrements the counting semaphore and each V (signal) increments it, so only the net count matters.

steps.title: Interpretation
steps.body: The value is positive, so 2 more P operations can proceed without blocking.

optionAnalysis.reason: $7+20+15$: treats P as an increment.
Ignores the net $-5$ change.
$7-15+20$: swaps P and V.

pitfalls: Mixing up P (decrement) with V (increment).
cse-1992-a-2-x.verification: Order does not matter for the final value: $7+15-20=2$.
